statement: A running model, not a calibrated one. Its leaf season, leaf size, the wood that flowers, the thickest support it has been seen to twine and the size of flower and berry behind its head and cluster come from published descriptions of the species or of this cultivar; the reach of an unsupported shoot is held inside the published range for stem twiners. Its rates, counts, stiffnesses and chances are this project’s choices, set so that a plant on the specimen frame reads, year by year, as the plant those descriptions and photographs of trained plants show; none has been measured on a plant. It is still thinner than the wisteria model in one respect: how a shoot chooses its way at a junction is copied from it. Use its output to compare scenarios and to show what a design implies, not to predict dates, sizes or loads.

names.basis: Two leaf forms, after Bean: "lower pairs of leaves stalked, uppermost ones almost or quite stalkless". The stalked leaf is the ordinary one, of the climbing and long shoots, and needs no name; the stalkless one is named for the flowering side shoots. The head is terminal and stalked (Bean: "at the end of the shoot, forming a terminal stalked inflorescence"), so it carries on the line of its shoot: facing out. The berries sit stalkless in the place of the flowers (BSBI account of the species), so the cluster is held as the head was.

phenology.budburstDoy.basis: The day shoots begin to lengthen, not the day leaves appear: the leaves of this species start to open in January (phenology.leafFlushDoy). Lengthening is taken to begin on 1 March. No dated source.

phenology.growthEndDoy.basis: Bean says this cultivar flowers into October on growth made after a winter cut, so shoots are taken to go on lengthening to the end of September. No dated source.

phenology.leafFlushDoy.basis: Of the species. Beckett and Beckett, Planting Native Trees and Shrubs (1979), as given by the Useful Temperate Plants database: new leaves often start to open in January and are well grown in April. The BSBI account of the species in Fermanagh (after Lang 1987): "New leaves open in December and January from bluish-green buds". Taken as 20 January to 15 April. The day in January is a choice, and is put after the middle of the month on purpose: the design report reads winter cover on 15 January and counts any leaf that has begun to open, and buds that have only just broken are not cover.

phenology.autumnColourDoy.basis: It has no autumn colour to speak of: the University of Connecticut plant database says of the species "no fall color". A slight dulling over the three weeks before the fall is assumed, so that the plant is seen to go over, the leaves still green when they drop. No dated source.

phenology.leafFallDoy.basis: Of the species. Beckett and Beckett (1979), as given by the Useful Temperate Plants database: the leaves fall in November. In sheltered places some stay green through the winter (Grime and others, in the BSBI account of the species in Fermanagh), which the engine cannot yet show: every leaf here is off by the end of November.

phenology.floralInitiationDoy.basis: Flower buds are taken to show about four weeks before the first heads open. No dated source.

phenology.flowerOpenDoy.basis: Bean’s supplement says of this cultivar that it "will flower from June to October"; nurseries give July to September; the BSBI account has the wild plant flowering from May to late September with peaks in early June and in September. Heads open from 7 June to 22 September here, and the last go over in mid October. The days within the months are a choice.

phenology.petalFallDoy.basis: Not used for this plant while each head has its own length of life (phenology.flowerLastsDays). Kept inside the flowering months.

phenology.flowerLastsDays.basis: How long one head is in flower, first flower to last. Each flower lasts two or three days, white on its first evening and yellow from the next (BSBI account of the species, after Knight 1996), and the flowers of a head open on successive evenings; the US plant patent of the most similar cultivar, ‘Scentsation’ (PP16,240), gives about two weeks. Not measured on this cultivar.

extension.leaderMPerSeason.basis: Bean calls this cultivar "exceptionally vigorous"; the US plant patent of the most similar cultivar, ‘Scentsation’ (PP16,240), gives a growth rate of 1 to 2 m a year; the RHS gives 4 to 8 m in 5 to 10 years. The middle of the patent’s figure. Not measured on this cultivar.

extension.lateralMPerSeasonByOrder.basis: Scaled down from the leader by the order of the branch. Not measured.

extension.whipMPerSeason.basis: The long shoots of the year that stand clear of the support (the RHS honeysuckle guide’s "wayward long shoots"), taken to grow a little slower than a leader. Not measured.

extension.establishmentFactorByYear.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

architecture.trunkStemStartYears.basis: Stems from the base: two in the first season and one more in each of the next two. The RHS honeysuckle guide has the shoots cut back by two thirds at planting to make a framework of several stems. How many is a choice.

architecture.nurseryCaneM.basis: A nursery plant on a short cane, as climbers are sold. Not measured.

architecture.maxBranchOrder.basis: A stem from the base, its branches, and two further orders of branch. The species is described as much-branched (BSBI account). The number is a choice.

architecture.leaderLengthM.basis: The RHS ultimate-height band of this cultivar (4 to 8 m) used as a cap on the length of a stem. A height band is not a route length, so this is a stand-in.

architecture.lateralLengthMByOrder.basis: Scaled down from the leader by the order of the branch. The RHS gives an ultimate spread of 1 to 1.5 m and a nursery 2 m; a branch follows the lattice and so is longer than the spread it makes. Not measured.

architecture.lateralLengthSpread.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

architecture.lateralChanceByParentOrder.basis: A branch at most of the junctions a stem passes: the buds stand in pairs at every node and the species is described as much-branched (BSBI account). The chances are a choice.

architecture.budExtraDormancyChance.basis: About a third of the buds that will make a branch wait a year or two first. A choice, lower than the wisteria model’s half because this plant leafs and branches from old wood readily.

architecture.maxStemsPerRoute.basis: The stems of this species wrap round their support and round each other (BSBI account: they twine "tightly around supporting stems (or around itself)"), so one lath or cable carries several; photographs show four to six old stems twisted together as a rope (reference stem-liana). Five is a choice.

architecture.maxStemsPerPrimaryMember.basis: See architecture.maxStemsPerRoute: one more on a stout member. A choice.

routing.occupancyCost.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

routing.downhillCostPerM.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

routing.uphillBonusPerM.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

routing.straightOnBonus.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

routing.riserBonus.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

routing.tierBonus.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

routing.roleDropChance.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

routing.noise.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

routing.giveUpCost.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

attachment.maxGraspDiameterMm.basis: Of the species. Darwin, The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants (1875): "Our English twiners, as far as I have seen, never twine round trees, excepting the honeysuckle (Lonicera periclymenum), which I have observed twining up a young beech-tree nearly 4 1/2 inches in diameter". One observation of a support the plant did hold, used here as its limit: the true limit is not known and may be greater. The taxon profile leaves the limit unknown.

attachment.minPitchM.basis: The rise of one turn of the coil on a slender support. This species coils closely enough to distort the young stems it climbs (BSBI account), and no measurement of its coil was found. 0.24 m is a choice, and a loose one: the engine stores a stem as points 40 mm apart, so a closer coil would be drawn as a zigzag.

attachment.pitchPerCircumference.basis: The rise of one turn on a stout support, in circumferences of that support. No measurement was found; a little closer than the wisteria model’s 1.46, as a choice.

organs.leafSpacingM.basis: Stem between one pair of leaves and the next. No flora read gives an internode length. Chosen so that a flowering side shoot 0.12 to 0.45 m long carries two to eight pairs; the long shoots of the real plant have longer internodes than its side shoots, which one figure cannot show. The engine lays a stem down in steps of 40 mm, so pairs stand 40 or 80 mm apart.

organs.leafLengthM.basis: Of the species. Bean (Trees and Shrubs Online): leaves "1 1/2 to 2 1/2 in. long", in metres. The Flora of the Burren gives 3 to 7 cm, the Flora of New Zealand 3 to 9 cm. No measurement of this cultivar was found.

organs.leavesPerNode.basis: Of the species. BSBI account: leaves "in opposite pairs", with "each pair at right-angles to the next". The engine sets every pair in the same plane.

organs.spurChance.basis: Not used for this plant: its short leafy shoots are grown as flowering side shoots (sideShoots), which carry their leaves in pairs and end in the flower head. A spur here would be a tuft of leaves with no flower.

organs.spurLengthM.basis: Not used for this plant: see organs.spurChance.

organs.spurLeafCount.basis: Not used for this plant: see organs.spurChance.

organs.racemeLengthM.basis: The width of a flower head, tip of one flower to tip of the one opposite. The flowers are 40 to 50 mm long (BSBI account, after Sell and Murrell; Bean: 1 1/2 to 2 in.) and stand out all round the end of the stalk, so a head is about twice that across. The US plant patent of the most similar cultivar, ‘Scentsation’ (PP16,240), gives 100 to 120 mm. Worked out from the flower, not measured on this cultivar.

organs.whipShareOfNodes.basis: The share of older leaf nodes that throw a long shoot in a year. A choice. Kept low because the engine neither sheds a long shoot nor lets it bear side shoots in later years, so each stays as a bare stem.

organs.whipsPerYearMax.basis: A cap on new long shoots a year. A choice: see organs.whipShareOfNodes.

organs.whipLengthM.basis: Length of a long shoot of the year. The RHS honeysuckle guide speaks of "wayward long shoots" without a length; the growth of a year is 1 to 2 m (extension.leaderMPerSeason) and a shoot with nothing to hold is taken to stop sooner. A choice.

organs.leafLifespanYears.basis: Deciduous (RHS record of this cultivar): a leaf lasts the season it grew in.

organs.clearStemHeightM.basis: The RHS honeysuckle guide describes established plants as "congested and bare at the bottom". How much stem is bare is a choice.

flowering.competenceYears.basis: Taken to flower from its second season. No source read states an age.

flowering.maturityRamp.basis: Fewer heads in its first two flowering years. A choice.

flowering.spurFloralChance.basis: Not used for this plant: it has no spurs (organs.spurChance).

flowering.unprunedFactor.basis: Not used for this plant: it applies to flower buds on spurs, and this plant has none.

flowering.currentSeasonFlowersPerM.basis: Heads borne directly at the nodes of a stem, for each metre of it: on the growth of the year, which is what lets this cultivar flower after a winter cut (Bean), and on last year’s stems, where they stand for the shortest flowering shoots. Most heads are borne at the ends of side shoots (sideShoots). A choice.

flowering.currentSeasonMinShootM.basis: A shoot that has made less than this in the year is taken not to flower along its length. A choice.

pruning.summerLeavesKept.basis: Not used for this plant: the summer cut to five or six leaves is the wisteria routine. The RHS prunes this plant after flowering, by a third (pruning group 11), which the engine does not yet act on.

pruning.winterBudsKept.basis: Not used for this plant: see pruning.summerLeavesKept.

regrowth.shootsPerCut.basis: New shoots from a stem cut hard back. The RHS guide renovates an old plant by cutting every stem to 60 cm and choosing among the new shoots that follow, so a stub is taken to throw two or three. The number is a choice.

thickening.tipRadiusSquaredMm2.basis: A young shoot about 2.5 mm thick. The species has "twining, thin stems" (University of Connecticut plant database); no flora read gives a thickness, and none was measured.

thickening.radiusSquaredPerMetreMm2.basis: Chosen so that a main stem carrying some 60 m of growth is about 30 mm thick at its base. No measurement of an old stem was found.

thickening.branchShare.basis: Copied from the Wisteria sinensis model for want of anything better. Not a measurement or a description of this plant.

fruit.setShare.basis: The share of heads that leave a cluster of berries. The RHS record of this cultivar has "Berries red"; no source read says how freely. Under half, as a choice.

fruit.lengthM.basis: The width of a cluster of berries. A berry is "8 mm diameter" and the berries are "stalkless in tight clusters" (BSBI account); a photograph of a cluster holds some twenty berries in a dome about four berries across (reference fruit-ripe-unripe-chapeltoun). Worked out from the berry and the photograph, not measured. Kept narrow because the cluster is drawn to this size whatever its number of berries.

fruit.swellDays.basis: Days from the last flower of a head to full-sized green berries. No source read gives it. Flowers of June give ripe berries by mid to late August (BSBI account); two to three weeks is taken for swelling, and kept short so that the berries of the last heads are full grown inside the ripening window.

fruit.ripenDoy.basis: Berries "are ripe from mid- to late-August onwards" (BSBI account). The window runs from 15 August to 2 November so that the berries of the last heads still ripen in their own year: the engine holds fruit that is full grown after the window green until the next one. The engine also spreads ripening to the end of the window, so most clusters here are red in October, later than the real plant; a real berry ripens some weeks after its own flower, which a window of dates cannot say.

fruit.fallDoy.basis: Birds take the berries through the autumn, some fruit "remaining on the plant until October or even early November" (BSBI account). From 7 September to 26 November, the later end allowing for the berries of the last heads.

appendages.tendrilNodePattern.basis: A stem twiner (RHS record: "A large twining deciduous climber"): it has no tendrils.

appendages.leafStalkCoilShare.basis: A stem twiner (RHS record): its leaf stalks do not coil. The upper leaves have almost no stalk (Bean).

appendages.aerialRootPatchSpacingM.basis: A stem twiner (RHS record): it has no clinging rootlets. Stems that lie on the ground root at intervals (BSBI account), which is not climbing.

appendages.prickleSpacingM.basis: Unarmed: Go Botany records the twigs of the species as without spines, prickles or thorns.

sideShoots.bearingWoodAgeYears.basis: RHS honeysuckle guide: honeysuckles of this pruning group flower "on short sideshoots on the previous season’s growth". Wood a year old or more bears them.

sideShoots.perMetrePerYear.basis: New side shoots a year on each metre of stem old enough to bear them. Buds stand in pairs at every node, so a metre of stem with some fifteen to twenty nodes could throw twice that; the engine lets a node bear one shoot at a time. A choice, set so that a plant five or six years old clothes the specimen frame (2.4 m of trellis and a post 3 m tall) as a mass of leaf, as the RHS describes an established plant ("congested", "overgrown thickets" if left) and as photographs of plants on walls and trellis show (reference habit-harlow, habit-trellis-boreham); no count was found.

sideShoots.lengthM.basis: The RHS calls them short. Flowering shoots in photographs carry four to eight pairs of leaves below the head, 0.15 to 0.5 m (reference scentsation-3, habit-harlow); no flora read gives a figure. A choice.

sideShoots.lifespanYears.basis: A side shoot is taken to leaf and flower for six seasons before it is shaded out or replaced. On the real plant it branches and becomes part of the tangle of thin stems that photographs show inside the leaf (reference habit-trellis-boreham, winter-geograph); the engine cannot fork it. A choice.

sideShoots.terminalFlowerShare.basis: The share of side shoots that end in a flower head in a year. The inflorescence is terminal (Bean: "at the end of the shoot, forming a terminal stalked inflorescence") and UConn says this cultivar "reliably produces ample quantities" of flowers; the share is a choice.

mechanics.greenShootModulusMPa.basis: Not measured on this plant. The growing end of a woodbine shoot is soft and limp: it revolves, and twines round its own older stems or round itself when it finds nothing else (BSBI account: stems twine "tightly around supporting stems (or around itself)"). Taken at half the generic 300 MPa, below the least stiff searcher base Hattermann and others 2022 measured (213 MN/m2), since the growing end is softer than any base. A choice.

mechanics.woodSetDays.basis: Not measured. The long shoots of this cultivar go on lengthening and flowering into October (Bean: "if cut back in winter will flower from June to October"), green and pliant for most of the summer; two months for a stretch to set is taken instead of the generic month. A choice.

mechanics.searcherReachM.basis: Hattermann and others 2022 give stem twiners the widest range of searcher reach, "from 10 cm to 225 cm"; Lonicera japonica was among their species but the paper as read gives no figure for it. 0.8 m is taken for the slender, soft shoots of this plant, which flop and wind round each other in photographs (reference stem-liana, fruit-dpc01). A choice inside the published range.

mechanics.leafFreshMassPerAreaKgM2.basis: Not weighed. A thin, soft deciduous leaf ("slightly downy or glabrous", Bean), lighter than the generic 0.2 kg/m2 for a broad leaf with its stalk. A choice.

mechanics.inflorescenceFreshMassKg.basis: Not weighed. A head of 6 to 15 flowers (BSBI account), each a slender tube 40 to 50 mm long and some 3 mm across with its lips, taken at a quarter of a gram each with the stalk and ovaries: about 4 g. Worked out, not weighed.

mechanics.fruitFreshMassKg.basis: Not weighed. A cluster of berries "8 mm diameter" (BSBI account): a sphere of 8 mm holds 0.27 cm3, so fifteen berries of fresh fruit at about the density of water weigh about 4 g. Worked out from the published diameter and an assumed count (morphology fruit.berriesPerCluster).

tropism.turnPerM.basis: Not measured. A twiner's shoot sweeps round and leans rather than standing plumb; about half the generic 1.5 rad/m, so that unsupported shoots arch and hang, as they do over the top of a trellis in photographs (reference habit-harlow, habit-trellis-boreham). A choice.

attachment.graspReachM.basis: Not measured on this plant. The sweep of a revolving shoot tip; Darwin (1875) gives the sweep of a hop at 19 inches across. A little above the generic 0.12 m, since this species twines readily round neighbouring stems and itself (BSBI account). A choice.

organs.leafTurnToOpenShare.basis: Leaves stand in pairs with their faces to the open side of a wall or trellis in photographs of trained plants (reference habit-harlow, habit-trellis-boreham); a little more than the generic half. Read from photographs, not measured.

organs.sideShootLeafLengthM.basis: The leaves of the short flowering shoots are the plant's smaller ones: Bean gives the species 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 in. (38 to 64 mm) and the uppermost pairs "almost or quite stalkless"; the Flora of New Zealand has the uppermost leaves small and suborbicular. Taken a little below Bean's range at its lower end. A choice.

organs.sideShootLeafSpacingM.basis: Stem between pairs on a flowering side shoot. No flora read gives an internode; photographs of flowering shoots show four to eight pairs in 0.15 to 0.3 m below the head (reference scentsation-3, habit-harlow), 0.03 to 0.05 m apart. The engine lays stems in steps of 0.04 m.

organs.sideShootLeavesPerNode.basis: Of the species. BSBI account: leaves "in opposite pairs", as on every shoot of the plant.

sideShoots.extensionMPerYear.basis: The short flowering shoots of one year lengthen in the next and become part of the tangle of thin stems (photographs: reference habit-trellis-boreham, stem-liana); the engine cannot let them fork, so they are let grow on instead. Not measured. A choice.

sideShoots.maxLengthM.basis: A side shoot grown on for several years is taken to stop at 0.5 m, the longest a new one makes: past that, a shoot of this plant leans over and winds into the tangle (reference habit-trellis-boreham, stem-liana), which the engine cannot draw for a shoot that has set as it stood. A choice.

sideShoots.branchAngleDeg.basis: Flowering shoots stand out from their stems at wide angles in photographs of trained plants (reference habit-harlow), the more so from level stems. Read from photographs, not measured.

sideShoots.breakSpreadDays.basis: The buds of this species break from January (BSBI account: new leaves open "in December and January"), and shoots go on breaking into spring. Five or six weeks after the day shoots begin to lengthen (phenology.budburstDoy) is a choice.

sideShoots.startTowardsLight.basis: The flowering shoots lean out from their stems and only then turn up to the light at their ends (reference habit-harlow, habit-trellis-boreham); less than the generic quarter, so that shoots from a level member do not set out as a row standing upright. A choice.

sideShoots.baseDiameterMm.basis: Not measured. The species has "thin stems" (University of Connecticut plant database); a flowering shoot of 0.45 m is taken to be 3 mm thick at its foot, tapering to the 2.5 mm of a young tip (thickening.tipRadiusSquaredMm2). A choice.

flowering.firstFlushDays.basis: Heads at the ends of side shoots from last year's wood (RHS honeysuckle guide: flowers "on short sideshoots on the previous season's growth") are taken to open in the eight or nine weeks from 7 June, the main flush. The BSBI account has the wild plant in full sun peaking in early June and again in September; Bean has this cultivar flowering "from June to October". The length of the flush is a choice.

flowering.repeatMaxPerSeason.basis: On the real plant a shoot whose terminal head has gone over grows on from the buds below it and ends in a later head (the BSBI account's second peak, in September; Bean: "from June to October"). The engine can say this only as a second head at the same place, which is how it is said here: once in a season. A choice.

flowering.repeatIntervalDays.basis: Days from a head going over to the later head on the same shoot opening: from the July end of the first flush to the September peak of the BSBI account is four to nine weeks. Worked out from that account's two peaks, not measured.

flowering.repeatShare.basis: The share of shoots whose first head is followed by a later one. Not counted on any plant; less than half, so that the later flowering is the lighter one, as the BSBI account and nurseries describe it (a main summer show, then a succession). A choice.

mechanics.woodModulusMPa.basis: Not measured on this plant. Hattermann and others 2022 measured 213 to 15 479 MN/m2 at the base of searcher shoots of 29 climbers and found about 3000 needed to hold a reach of more than about 0.8 m; the slender stems of this twiner flop and wind round each other in photographs (reference stem-liana, fruit-dpc01) rather than standing out, so half that is taken. A choice inside the published range.
